627.t: Will young players take up old-time fiddling
627.s: The interviewer asks whether youngsters will play Cage's kind of fiddle music; Cage says not many.
627.ch: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling

627.t: Everyone's names recorded for the tape; young people prefer new music
627.s: The interviewer gets names from all present for the record, including Robert Pete Williams and Dick Allen, and notes nobody else plays old-time fiddle locally; Cage says youngsters do not play his kind.
627.ch: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
627.q: No, they don't play my kind.

968.s: He says the music is going backward; the older players cared more, while today's learn for free.
968.q: No Bill. It's getting more, it's going back for the, for the music playing. Before that time Bill, we used to play really understanding music.

910.t: Jazz then and now: music as food, and golf
910.s: He compares the evolution of jazz to changing food as nourishment for the mind; light chatter about golf and weather.
910.q: They had, from the ‘20s, well you can go back to say 1910 and start coming up and it started changing there, and then it started getting more sophisticated and more educated with the like Fletcher Henderson, and that came along and then all of a sudden bebop came out and that came for a while and…

537.t: The blues disappearing from jazz and young stars
537.s: He laments that publicists and licks have replaced paid dues and the blues, citing Freddie Hubbard's development.
537.q: No, no, no, no. I’m going to think of it. Because Bill Fielder was telling me about that, that he and Freddie were in — Slide Hampton.

605.t: Self-indulgence, learning languages and flattening of expression
605.s: Dobbins sees self-indulgence widely, discusses learning languages, and says media flatten speech and music.
605.q: A lot. I mean I not only notice it with students, I notice it in many, many professional musicians that have major record contracts and things too. Yeah, sure. And in fact one of the things that I find missing in music more and more — well one of the things I wanted to say too that’s related to the…

548.s: Jazz risks becoming a museum piece; he names Dave Douglas and the Knitting Factory crowd as innovators.
548.q: Well I mean there’s a lot in musical terms that could be developed that hasn’t been in terms of even harmony in terms of extended forms, compositionally, I mean there’s a whole lot of things that could be done. And it is being done and it will be done and all that, but I think that this at…

588.t: Young artists who might carry the tradition
588.s: She hasn't heard anyone with the individuality of the past.
588.q: I think a lot of the young men are doing this. I haven't heard anybody who reminds me -- not do songs like Dinah Washington, but who -- you know what I mean? Ella Fitzgerald or Sarah or -- I haven't heard anybody yet. Cassandra Wilson has a song and Diane Reeves, but I'm talking about -- I don't…

471.t: Esperanza Spalding and the future of jazz
471.s: Cobb says jazz will last but young players may lack the seasoning.
471.ch: Kind of Blue business and anniversary tours
471.q: I think the talent – all through this music, there’s going to be people that come up and come to the top, because the people love this music. It’s going to always be jazz music. It’s al[ways] going to be. I don’t know how popular it might ever be. It might be like it has always been, up and down,…

555.t: Young women today don't know the struggle
555.s: They agree today's young women have not been through what they did, though good ones come along now and then.
555.q: There are some girls that are very good. The bass player . . .

373.t: Will jazz last? Aaron Weinstein and the need for leaders
373.s: He argues jazz will not die so long as young players like Aaron Weinstein learn from elders, though it needs new leaders.
373.ch: Freelancing, politics and New York clubs
373.q: It’s not a matter of keeping it that way. I don’t think Bach is out of fashion. When people can play Bach or Haydn or Mozart or Bartok – there’s a 20-year – he must be 21 years old now, a violinist named Aaron Weinstein. His first recording was from a very good label called Arbors. Fortunately the…

705.s: He explains going back to ancestors to go forward, Egyptian ideas of music and planets, and the loss of human contact through machines.
705.q: That wonderful book that Dr. Wayne Chandler wrote, which says that in order for us to go ahead we have got to go back. It’s like…I’m sure we all have the same experience. Mom and Pop told us some things when we were younger which we either rejected or we didn’t understand. When we become older,…

426.t: Why multi-track and easy fixes weakened the spontaneity of music
426.s: He argues that overdub fixing and cheap machines reduce emotion and spontaneity compared to live two-track recording.
426.q: Well, there are two phases of that. One is that we set it up the way we think it should be, to get the best sound. That would be the first thing, and then what they are comfortable with. Those things are generally at odds. What is good for sound was not good for playing. Now, in the advent of…

231.t: Why vaudeville quality was better than today's
231.s: He says performers then had to be clever and versatile for less pay, while today anyone is hired and paid more.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: They ain't got nothing to offer today. Don't talk about today. We're talking now about over 25 years ago. If you're talking about now over 25 years ago, you can't match that with today. Because today nothing is like it was then. 'Cause you had to have more to offer then than you have to today.
